formattedActions.title: Develop Shared Commitments, Political Alignment and Ownership
formattedActions.description: This Action includes guidance and tools to help national, subnational and city governments to jointly establish shared political commitment, collective ownership and long-term alignment required to support multilevel climate finance and implementation.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Multilevel climate action starts with shared political commitment. Joint commitment processes can create a common mission, clarify roles across governance levels, and build the mandate, trust and institutional relationships needed for later stages of investment planning, finance mobilization, implementation and learning. In practice, they help move climate action from isolated pledges toward coordinated, network-based governance.

pathways.title: Joint Political Commitments, Dialogues and Coalitions
pathways.whatItIs: Joint political commitment dialogues and coalition mechanisms provide a recurring process through which national, subnational and city governments can establish a shared vision, align climate priorities and create long-term coalitions for coordinated climate action and investment. They help create a collaborative governance arrangement to clarify institutional roles and responsibilities, aligns actors around a common mission, and establishes a shared mandate for implementation of climate projects.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Joint political commitments and coalitions establish the governance foundation for subsequent investment planning, finance mobilisation, implementation and continuous learning by reducing institutional fragmentation, strengthening vertical policy coherence and fostering collective ownership of climate objectives across multiple levels of government.
transferability: Joint political commitment mechanisms can be adapted to different governance contexts by:

Develop a joint political commitment and dialogue process where cities and national agencies have the capacity to coordinate and sustain the commitment. In Sweden, the joint commitment process of the Climate City Contracts works because municipalities are powerful actors, the process is renewed annually, and the framework can be used to understand governing and supporting processes across local, regional, national and European levels.

Where local capacity is uneven, start with recurring multilevel dialogue, with an ambition to move towards a full CCC-like process. The Town Hall COPs in Africa show that a lighter, dialogue-based model can still generate commitments, national buy-in and policy inputs feeding into NDCs and NAPs.

Allow cities to enter at different readiness levels. Structure the process with mandatory commitments for all cities and optional commitments that cities can join based on their readiness, as shown by the Transition Arena model. That makes transferability stronger, because it gives countries a common floor while still allowing different cities to move at different speeds and with different tools.

Build from pioneer municipalities in context with low readiness levels. In contexts where national coordination exists unevenly or is not strong enough to sustain long-term joint commitments, a national government help build momentum by backing a few municipalities that are already willing to move ahead, then help them work as a cluster and share experience.

Aligning commitments with existing political and budgeting cycles so that political commitments become part of routine government decision-making. Periodic reviews can then be used to update commitments based on implementation progress and emerging political priorities.
Embedding regular review and renewal processes to maintain political ownership, strengthen accountability and adapt commitments as implementation progresses.
enablingConditions: A shared long-term mission or national strategy that provides a common direction for national and subnational governments while allowing flexibility in local implementation.
Political will of both national and local leadership, ensuring that political commitments are jointly owned and can be sustained beyond electoral cycles.
Clearly defined institutional roles and responsibilities so that each participating actor understands its contribution and accountability.

illustrativeExamples.title: Town Hall COPs
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Town Hall COPs are a strong emerging example of how multilevel dialogues and commitments can help bridge local implement...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Town Hall COPs are a strong emerging example of how multilevel dialogues and commitments can help bridge local implementation with national climate strategy and planning.  Launched by ICLEI Africa in 2025, the format gives local governments and communities a dedicated space to discuss climate goals, jointly review progress and identify next steps in line with national plans and global commitments. The Town Halls also bring in national government representatives (with national presence recorded at 60% of events) so local priorities could be heard directly and fed into NDC and NAP implementation. By October 2025, 18 Town Hall COPs were convened, engaging over 2000 participants, across six Sub-Saharan African countries. These participants ranged from mayors and national agency officials to the youth and civil society. The dialogues helped develop and surface over 300 local commitments. In South Africa, the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment became the first national government to recognise the model as a platform for inclusive national climate planning and local implementation of the NDC, Building on this endorsement, ICLEI Africa and the South African Local Government Association (SALGA) rolled out the Town Halls across the country to enable multilevel dialogues and subsequent commitments, which feed back into policy, implementation and reporting. Click here to know more about the Town Hall COPs.

illustrativeExamples.title: The Joint Commitment process of the Climate City Contracts (CCC)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: The Joint Commitment process of the Climate City Contracts (CCC) demonstrates how joint political commitment can be turn...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Joint Commitment process of the Climate City Contracts (CCC) demonstrates how joint political commitment can be turned into a recurring multilevel governance arrangement rather than a one-off declaration. The contract process is built around a shared climate-neutrality mission and an annual cycle in which cities, Viable Cities and national agencies each make commitments, review progress and renew priorities. The city’s role is to gather the wider transition arena, which includes a space for collaboration, coordination and dialogue among public and private actors who need to help deliver the transition and connect local action to national support. The contract itself is structured in three linked parts — climate goals, a roadmap or portfolio of actions, and a climate investment plan — so political commitment is tied to implementation planning and financing. Through a joint commitment mechanism, the Climate City Contracts process is designed to work through a broader network of businesses, academia, civil society and public organizations, helping shift municipalities from traditional governance toward a more network-based model.

formattedActions.title: Assess Enabling Environments
formattedActions.description: This Action will provide foundational assessment tools to identify and improve the policy, fiscal, data and coordination conditions needed for national, subnational and city governments to plan, access and deploy urban climate finance. It will help users diagnose barriers to climate investment readiness, including gaps in financing architecture, intergovernmental transfers, subnational borrowing, data systems, coordination, private finance mobilization and project bankability.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Multilevel climate investment depends on enabling conditions across data, policy, budget and finance, and coordination. Assessing enabling environments can therefore help identify and improve the readiness of national, subnational and city governments to jointly plan investments, implement portfolios and pipelines, mobilize finance and build capacities. Enabling environments also shape the ability of private financial actors to identify, structure, finance and implement climate investment opportunities.

pathways.title: National and subnational enabling environments assessments
pathways.whatItIs: Assessment of enabling environments helps unpack the conditions that affect urban climate finance in specific national and subnational contexts. It examines climate policy, budget and finance, climate data, and vertical and horizontal coordination, then translates the findings into recommendations, reform priorities and, where relevant, roadmaps or blueprints for follow-up action. The national tool is aimed primarily at national officials, while the subnational tool is designed for cities and other subnational governments; the two are meant to be used together where possible so the enabling environment can be assessed across levels of government.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Multilevel climate investment depends on enabling conditions being in place across data, policy, budget and finance, and coordination — yet these are often weak, uneven or invisible to decision-makers, leaving national, subnational and city governments unsure where the readiness gaps lie. To this end, enabling environment assessments surface where those conditions fall short, consolidate them into a comparable readiness profile, and channel the findings into concrete reforms, so the diagnostic feeds directly into investment planning, finance mobilisation and implementation rather than remaining a standalone report.
transferability: The EFC Tools provide a standardised approach, but applying them in a new jurisdiction requires tailoring to context rather than direct replication:

Adapt the assessment methodology to context. Where subnational climate, fiscal and governance data are limited, lean on interviews and policy review — as the India pilot did with its desk review and seven stakeholder interviews — while reflecting the real intergovernmental relationships in play where mandates are unclear, and calibrating the access-to-finance analysis to the actual depth of local financial systems and intermediation.

Deploy the National and Subnational Tools together, so a new jurisdiction is assessed as a coherent multilevel system rather than at a single level in isolation, with the national baseline framing the subnational diagnosis, as in the India and Indonesia pilots.

Secure access to stakeholders and source documentation for the data-collection, inception and validation steps — the policies, budgets and officials the process depends on — much as the India pilot used its two New Delhi roundtables to confirm findings.

Ground the assessment in government ownership and existing planning and budget cycles, so its recommendations are taken up as live reforms; in India, the gaps mapped directly onto instruments already in use, such as Central Finance Commission grants and NMSH 2.0, rather than requiring new mechanisms.
Identify technical partners to run the workshops, interpret the scored dimensions and translate findings into roadmaps, as GIZ did alongside MoHUA, NIUA and TERI in the India pilot.
enablingConditions: Availability of governance, financial and climate-related data, since the depth of accessible data bounds what any assessment can conclude, and strengthening subnational climate data is itself one of the four EFC dimensions.
Institutional capacity and technical assistance to undertake the assessment and interpret findings — frequently a precondition rather than an optional add-on where in-house capacity is limited.
Coordination across national ministries, subnational governments and stakeholders, which the inception and final workshops are built to secure and which is itself a scored EFC dimension.
Political ownership and a mandate to act on findings, so recommendations are taken up rather than shelved — the reason the India pilot convened 80+ stakeholders in policy roundtables.

�� Alignment with existing policy, fiscal and financing frameworks, so reforms can be channelled through intergovernmental transfers, finance-commission grants and municipal budgeting rather than through entirely new mechanisms.

illustrativeExamples.fullText: National Enabling Framework Conditions (EFC) Tools offer a practical way to assess a national government against four key dimensions – policy, budget and finance, climate data, and vertical and horizontal coordination. These categories are further broken down into 16 sub-categories that include 64 assessment dimensions. The dimensions help identify priority areas for reform, and the process includes identifying stakeholders, collecting evidence, holding consultations, preparing results and identifying follow-up actions. The tool was piloted in India and Indonesia, making it a strong EMDE reference for how national enabling conditions can be assessed and translated into reform.

subExamples.title: The India pilot (2024)
subExamples.excerpt: The India pilot (2024) illustrates how the national tool works in practice. The pilot was led by GIZ, alongside the Indi...
subExamples.fullText: The India pilot (2024) illustrates how the national tool works in practice. The pilot was led by GIZ, alongside the Indian Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, the National Institute of Urban Affairs and The Energy Research Institute. It included a desk review with seven stakeholder interviews and two roundtables in New Delhi attended by more than 80 participants. The findings on the four dimensions included gaps in local institutional mandates, own-source revenues and borrowings, city-level climate data and coordination between state and local governments. Each gap points to a specific reform — broadening grants from the national finance commission to support climate action, for instance, or issuing city climate action plan guidelines under national missions. Another pilot in Indonesia runs the same tool with the national planning ministry (Bappenas) and pilot cities including Padang and Medan. By feeding directly into partners' capacity-building work with government stakeholders rather than sitting as a standalone report, both pilots turn the assessment into an input to reform. Click [here] to know more about the pilots.

formattedActions.title: Institutionalize Multilevel Governance Frameworks and National Platforms
formattedActions.description: This section will include guidance and tools to help national, subnational and city governments to institutionalize long-term multilevel governance by building coordination capabilities, strengthening institutional arrangements and creating the investment and implementation capacities needed to sustain climate transitions.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Institutionalizing multilevel climate investment is fundamentally about building long-term implementation capacity rather than creating one-off coordination mechanisms. Iterative coordination frameworks can help develop governance capabilities across institutions. These could be supported by nationally led coordination platforms capable of aligning governance, financing, project preparation, implementation actors and investment priorities across levels of government and the private sector, along with intermediary units for day-to-day coordination, monitoring, accountability and feedback loops. These arrangements also help strengthen institutional memory, leadership, trust, learning and feedback loops across organizations.

pathways.title: National Platforms
pathways.whatItIs: In the context of CHAMP, national platforms are best understood as nationally owned and led initiatives for long-term coordination and implementation of climate action. Their purpose is to align political leadership, sectoral planning, finance and implementation around a shared national strategy, while creating a dedicated space for subnational governments, cities, development partners and other actors to work through priorities together. These platforms can be designed to bring urban and subnational priorities into the core of the process, so cities are not treated as downstream implementers but as co-shapers of priorities, pipelines and delivery arrangements. A useful way to think about them is as an enabling architecture for moving from fragmented, project-by-project action to a more programmatic, systemic approach.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Cities and subnational governments often face misalignment with national climate and development priorities, limited entry points into decision-making, weak project pipelines, and fiscal and creditworthiness constraints that make climate finance hard to access. To this end, a national platform creates a space for local and national actors to align policies, pipelines and finance across levels of government so urban climate action can move from fragmented projects to a more programmatic delivery model.,
transferability: Host the national platform within suitable institutions according to the governance context. Depending on the level of decentralization and governance arrangements, the platform may be coordinated by a group public and institutional partners, such as Viable Cities, a ministry-led multi-stakeholder platform such as citiES 2030, or a country-led financing framework that is designed to work across national and subnational levels, as in Tanzania.

Adapt the platform functions and mandates to national priorities and capacities.  Countries can prioritize different functions, from initial engagement and program readiness to investment planning, financing and implementation, and adjust the operations of the platform to match their challenges and ambitions.

Bring cities into the platform through mechanisms that fit the governance system. In settings with high local capacities, city mobilization can be direct, as in Viable Cities’ Climate City Contracts. In less capacitated contexts, city mobilization can be routed through national processes while local governments build their own capacities and frameworks over time and continuously engage the national government through multilevel dialogues, as in Tanzania.

Adopt an iterative, learning-by-doing approach where the prioritized strategies and initiatives could first be tested before a full roll-out, especially in context where institutional capacities are limited, as in Tanzania.
enablingConditions: Strong national leadership mandate, cross-government commitment and durable support from a wider political and social base.
Regular consultation with subnational leaders, sectoral working groups, and clear channels for cities to feed into national planning
Institutional capacity and continuity, including a capable coordinating team, clear roles, and sustained staffing, resources and institutional support over time.
Subnational readiness, including subnational and city-level climate and financial plans, data, and support to develop investable pipelines and integrate climate into budgets
Participation of national and multilateral development banks and the private sector to support through innovative, catalytic and concessional finance.

illustrativeExamples.fullText: citiES 2030 is a strong example of a nationally anchored, multilevel and multi-stakeholder coordination platform that helps turn climate mission goals into implementation support for cities. It brings together cities, public sector actors, private sector partners, academia, civil society and citizens, and it works across European, national and local levels within the EU Cities Mission and Adaptation Mission. The platform provides services for learning and capacity building, Climate City Contract development, and the implementation of interconnected project portfolios and multi-city collaboration. In Spain, that support has helped five cities submit their Climate City Contracts and receive the EU Mission Label, showing how a platform can connect national coordination with concrete city-level implementation. illustrativeExamples.fullText: Viable Cities demonstrates how a nationally anchored platform can turn climate ambition into an ongoing multilevel implementation architecture rather than a one-off coordination exercise. In Sweden, Viable Cities works with 48 cities and six government agencies and coordinates the country’s participation in CHAMP. Through the Climate City Contract approach, Viable Cities helps align municipal commitments with national support, shared learning and implementation capacity. The platform’s value lies in that continuity – it connects local priorities to a national mission, creates a common framework for collaboration and implementation, and helps keep governance, planning and implementation moving together over time. illustrativeExamples.title: Tanzania’s Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Tanzania’s Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF) is a useful example to illustrate how a nationally led platfor...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Tanzania’s Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF) is a useful example to illustrate how a nationally led platform can be adapted across levels of government when it is paired with local ownership, iterative strategy-building and robust international cooperation for public and private finance. Rolled out on the mainland and in Zanzibar, the process aligned financing and development planning, broke silos within the Ministry of Finance and Planning, and used pilot dialogues with LGAs to surface locally appropriate financing solutions and bankable projects. INFF has demonstrated visible early results in Tanzania. Zanzibar’s revenue collection system is now used by 10 of 11 regional administrations, Zanzibar launched a USD 450 million sovereign sukuk, Tanga issued a USD 20.5 million water green bond, four SDG-aligned corporate bonds totalled USD 380 million, a USD 60 million road infrastructure bond to was issued to empower local contractors. Further, Zanzibar’s redesigned SDG Investor Map helped mobilize USD 5.5 million. Moreover, in coordination with national government via multilevel dialogues, Tanzanian cities like Dodoma have started developing their own local frameworks targeting local challenges and opportunities, such as improving local revenues.

Click here to know more.

illustrativeExamples.fullText: CCFLA’s Urban-Inclusive Country Platforms Framework provides guidance on how a nationally led platform can be designed to systematically integrate cities and other subnational actors into climate finance and implementation systems. The framework is built around the barriers that often keep urban priorities out of country platforms – misalignment between national and subnational priorities, weak project pipelines, limited fiscal capacity and creditworthiness, and the absence of city-focused instruments – and responds with a phased roadmap from initial engagement to program readiness, investment programming, financing and implementation. Implementing the framework by national governments would allow for regular engagement with subnational leaders, inclusion of urban ministries and local representatives in coordination structures, support for local climate action plans and project pipelines, aggregation of smaller urban projects, and use of concessional, blended and de-risking tools through intermediaries such as national development banks and local financial institutions. Click here to know more about the framework.

pathways.title: Overarching, Iterative Coordination Mechanisms
pathways.whatItIs: An overarching, iterative coordination framework provides the institutional architecture through which national, subnational and city governments, together with financial institutions, infrastructure providers, project developers and other implementation partners, can coordinate climate action and investment over the long term.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: An iterative framework can help build long-term institutional relationships – strengthening implementation capacity and creating continuous feedback loops between planning, financing and delivery. Implementing such a framework can help governments sustain climate transitions over time, rather than having one-off coordination or consultations.
transferability: Adapting coordination frameworks and processes to the country's governance systems, enabling countries and cities to define governance relationships, supporting processes and coordination arrangements that reflect their own institutional context. In centralized systems, a national ministry could lead coordination, while decentralized may distribute coordination responsibilities across regional or state governments working alongside cities.
Building on existing coordination mechanisms, such as climate or NDC units, national platforms, subnational climate cells or sectoral coordination bodies, rather than creating parallel institutions.

Applying the coordination mechanisms progressively, where countries with limited institutional capacities may begin with simpler multistakeholder dialogues and progressively institutionalize recurring coordination processes as governance capabilities develop.
enablingConditions: Long-term political and institutional leadership to sustain collaboration, coordination and implementation across electoral and funding cycles.
Clearly defined governance relationships, roles and supporting processes that enable actors across governance levels to coordinate effectively within their own institutional context.
Regular coordination forums, learning processes and feedback mechanisms that enable actors to share knowledge, coordinate actions and continuously refine implementation.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Colombia's  Strategic Committee on Cities and Climate Change illustrates how an overarching, iterative coordination fram...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Colombia's  Strategic Committee on Cities and Climate Change illustrates how an overarching, iterative coordination framework can support long-term multilevel climate governance. Co-hosted by the national government and WRI, the committee is not a one-off convening but the institutional architecture through which national authorities, subnational and city governments, and partners such as NGOs and funders coordinate climate action and investment over time. It operates through recurring cycles: a biannual forum brings these actors together to review city climate plans for alignment with national commitments such as Colombia's updated NDC and long-term strategy (E2050), identify active projects and synergies, prioritise high-impact and feasible measures, and connect them to enabling mechanisms — for example the Corridor of Climate Financing, a platform led by the National Planning Department that links climate projects to funders and provides support. By convening the same actors repeatedly rather than through one-off consultations, the framework builds long-term institutional relationships, strengthens implementation capacity and creates continuous feedback loops between planning, financing and delivery, helping the country address persistent political, financial and technical barriers and sustain its climate transition as circumstances evolve.

pathways.title: Intermediary Coordination, Facilitation and Accountability Function
pathways.whatItIs: An intermediary coordination function is a dedicated, trusted unit that helps move multilevel climate commitments from agreement to implementation. It sits between participating institutions and provides shared capacity for analysis, facilitation, strategic alignment, monitoring and learning. Why is it needed: The implementation of climate projects often spans siloed institutions with different mandates, resources and decision cycles. To this end, intermediary coordination functions are needed to avoid siloes, align mandates and help sustain coordination beyond specific projects, programs or funding cycles. They also help create institutional memory by through by enabling recurring coordination, documentation of processes and feedback loops, enabling strong institutional relationships, accountability and progressively improving multilevel climate governance system.
transferability: Anchor the function in existing institutions and systems, such as a ministry, national agency, climate platform, local-government association, city network or research body, and connect it to existing climate, intergovernmental, planning and budget processes rather than creating a parallel institutional structure.

Scale its functions to capacity and implementation needs. In lower-capacity contexts, begin with convening, issue tracking, documentation and implementation support. Functions such as analysis, governance diagnostics, policy and finance alignment, monitoring, knowledge management and adaptive learning can be added as needs and capacities evolve.

Maintaining clear institutional boundaries. The intermediary function should focus on analyses, facilitation and brokering alignment, while governments, financial institutions and delivery organisations retain their formal mandates and decision rights.
enablingConditions: A clear mandate, senior political and institutional sponsorship, and trust from national and subnational actors.
Dedicated staffing covering facilitation, policy, finance, implementation, data analysis and knowledge management.
Access to relevant implementation data and decision-makers, supported by common milestones, reporting routines and channels for resolving barriers and institutional frictions unresolved barriers
A recurring coordination and learning cycle linked to public planning, budgeting and implementation processes.
Organisational cultures that permit experimentation, reflection and adjustment.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Morocco's  4C Maroc (Competence Centre for Climate Change) demonstrates how a dedicated intermediary unit constituted as...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Morocco's 4C Maroc (Competence Centre for Climate Change) demonstrates how a dedicated intermediary unit constituted as an independent competence centre — rather than a line directorate within a ministry — can strengthen climate governance by acting as a neutral, multi-stakeholder platform. Formally established in 2016 as a public-interest group, and with a membership organised into four "colleges" spanning public institutions and local authorities, the private sector, research and training bodies, and civil society, it performs three complementary activities:
·      Strengthening the capacities of national actors across the climate agenda,
·      Capitalising knowledge on vulnerability, adaptation, mitigation and climate finance, and developing decision-support tools such as climate databases and vulnerability indicators,
·      Convening dialogue and coordination among diverse stakeholders while supporting the national greenhouse-gas monitoring system that underpins Morocco's UNFCCC reporting.

Through these activities, 4C Maroc performs the convening, facilitation, capacity-building and monitoring functions of an intermediary unit while remaining institutionally distinct from any single ministry, extending its reach through regional and pan-African outreach.

formattedActions.description: This section will include guidance and tools to support national, subnational and city governments in jointly planning climate investments, preparing projects and developing coordinated urban climate investment pipelines.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Climate-related investment planning, portfolio development and project preparation are linked steps in turning shared priorities into investment-ready pipelines. Joint investment planning helps identify investments priorities, portfolio development bundles the projects and related governance, regulatory and policy measures into a coherent package; and project preparation facilities then help project pipelines become bankable. Across all of this, coordination, orchestration and technical assistance are what keep the portfolio moving and reduce fragmentation across levels of government.

pathways.title: Joint Climate Investment Planning and Budgeting
pathways.whatItIs: Investment planning and budgeting are complementary activities that provide a recurring process through which national, subnational and city governments can translate shared climate goals into investment priorities, sequencing, responsibilities and indicative resource requirements. Joint investment planning helps identify which climate investments are required, who is expected to deliver and finance them, when they should occur, and how funding gaps and risks will be addressed. Once the investments are identified and planned, climate budgeting then involves integrating priority projects into operating and capital budgets of a municipality or higher levels of government, assigning implementation responsibilities and tracking delivery through the regular budget cycles. When undertaken jointly by national, subnational and local governments, these activities can help align local investment needs with national policies, funding programmes and fiscal decisions – strengthening coordinated climate action across levels of government.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Climate action plans may often set out actions without a clear understanding of their costs, financing responsibilities or links to regular budget decisions, which may contribute to the planning-to-investment gap faced by climate projects. Joint climate investment planning and budgeting can therefore help align priorities across levels of government, identify financing needs and gaps and embed agreed investments into routine operating and capital budgets so that climate commitments are translated into coordinated implementation.
transferability: Adapt to the governance context. Map where the city planning, budgeting and investment authority sits, and tailor the connections between local, regional and national processes accordingly. In more centralized systems, national or regional finance authorities may lead the investment planning and budgeting process while cities may provide locally grounded investment priorities and implementation evidence.

Develop progressively and expand the scope over time. Lower-capacity governments can begin with climate-aligned budget tagging, a priority investment register, and basic mapping of costs, responsibilities and funding gaps. As data and capacity improve, the process can incorporate more advanced investment planning that extends beyond municipal assets to utilities, households, businesses and regional or national infrastructure.
enablingConditions: Sustained political and administrative mandate. National, subnational and city leaders must authorise the investment planning and budgeting processes, connect it to agreed climate goals and sustain it across annual budget and electoral cycles.

Clear roles, responsibilities and decision pathways. Governments need agreement on who identifies, funds, approves, implements and monitors investments—including the respective responsibilities of national, subnational and local authorities and external actors.
Integration into existing financial planning and budgeting processes covering both operational and investment responsibilities

Monitoring, accountability and review. Responsibilities, expenditure and delivery should be monitored through ordinary budget and operational reporting, with findings used to update priorities, funding assumptions and future budgets.

pathways.title: Portfolio and Pipeline Development
pathways.whatItIs: Portfolio and pipeline development involves translating agreed climate priorities into a coordinated portfolio of interventions and progressively identifying and preparing the investible projects that emerge from it. A portfolio can package projects with enabling policy, governance, procurement, capacity and implementation measures around a common mission, through coordination and aggregation across city, regional and national levels. While not every portfolio intervention needs to be investible from the outset, portfolios can generate a pipeline of projects and investment opportunities that can then be prepared for financing. Therefore, portfolios represent a promising approach to crowd in finance and move from investment planning toward implementation.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: A project-by-project approach is often insufficient to scale climate investment and implementation. Countries and cities need a portfolio of interventions, with a pipeline of well-prepared projects, integrated with enabling regulations, governance functions, procurement, financing and implementation pathways. This can help turn individual initiatives into a well-connected, sequenced and bankable package of interventions. This way, a portfolio approach could make the path from concepts to implementation clearer and more visible for financiers and investors.
transferability: Tailor portfolio development to the national climate priorities and implementation capacities. Cities with relatively less capacities can start with mapping key actors, identifying and aligning projects with national priorities, and engaging with key actors, such as PPFs, then move to portfolio development and governance once the actors are involved and enabling conditions are mature.

Different lead institutions can host the portfolio and pipeline development. Depending on the governance setup, portfolio development and coordination role can sit within a national program or agency, regional authority, a multistakeholder body of local governments or external partners, such as city networks. The key is having sufficient mandate and convening power to continually develop and implement the portfolio.

Portfolio funding models can vary. Some contexts will need a donor-led or grant-led portfolio development, while others with higher levels of fiscal capacity can use city-led, national-led or blended funding arrangements. The key is having funding that is sufficient to develop the portfolio from planning to investment readiness.

Tailor outreach to PPFs to match sector priorities, country context and pipeline maturity, so early-stage projects are steered toward diagnostics and concept development, while more advanced pipelines are matched with structuring, de-risking and investment-readiness support.
enablingConditions: A clear mission, mandate and a coordination function. The portfolio needs a national-level mandate (e.g., through a national mission), alongside clear roles across levels of government and an intermediary team or similar coordination function to keep actors, including governments, project developers and financiers coordinated, track progress and revise the portfolio as conditions change.
National-local coordination mechanisms that allow city-level priorities and lessons to feed into national policy, investment programmes and funding decisions.
An investment plan or preliminary pipeline to work from, so the portfolio is built from agreed climate priorities across levels of government, rather than from siloed projects.
Early engagement with project preparation facilities, so that the portfolio and pipeline are prepared for bankability from the outset.

Reliable data and assessment capacity. Governments need sufficient data and technical capacity to identify projects across levels of government, assess readiness, identify gaps and structure a coherent theory of change across the portfolio.

illustrativeExamples.fullText: SOURCE is a project-preparation software platform. A joint initiative of the multilateral development banks coordinated by the not-for-profit Sustainable Infrastructure Foundation, SOURCE uses standardised, sector-specific question sets covering the full project lifecycle—aligned with the SDGs and the Paris Agreement—to help governments define, develop and manage sustainable infrastructure projects consistently and transparently, with the aim of improving bankability, crowding in private finance and strengthening public-sector capacity. The case demonstrates how a shared digital tool can standardise and de-risk project preparation across governments while linking prepared projects to preparation facilities and financiers. illustrativeExamples.fullText: System Demonstrators provide a systematic way for governments and funders to move beyond individual projects toward mission-driven urban transition portfolios. Rather than starting with a predefined list of projects, participating cities define a shared mission, map the system and structural barriers, convene relevant public, private and civic actors, and develop a coordinated portfolio of interventions across areas such as governance, infrastructure, regulation, procurement, finance, behaviour and technology. Not every intervention needs to be commercially investible; through implementation and learning, the portfolio can progressively surface projects and wider investment opportunities that are ready to move into project preparation and financing pipelines. In Lund, for example, a broader energy and mobility portfolio helped identify local energy systems as an emerging investment area, with EnergyNet representing one opportunity for further financing and implementation.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support c...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Box: What are Project Preparation Facilities?

Project Preparation Facilities (PPFs) are organizations, initiatives, or institutions that support cities in developing bankable, investment-ready projects, typically from a project’s concept, design, or scoping stage up to the financial close. A PPF may provide technical and/or financial support. PPFs can provide a wide range of support depending on a project’s stage and sector. The overarching goal of PPFs is preparing bankable, or investment-ready, projects. A project is bankable, whether from public or private sources, when its risk-return profile meets investors’ criteria. Key criteria include the probability of success, sufficient estimated cash flows to cover costs and produce returns that meet investor expectations, and whether the project will be implemented by a creditworthy entity.

formattedActions.title: Mobilize Finance, Shape Local Markets and Deliver Investment Portfolios
formattedActions.description: This section will include guidance and tools for national, subnational and city governments to mobilize and deploy catalytic funding to test and scale solutions, de-risking mechanisms to support urban climate projects and shape local markets using aggregated procurement.
formattedActions.systemsLogic: Implementing portfolios and pipelines often requires interconnected financing, implementation and market-shaping mechanisms operating together as part of a system. Catalytic and de-risking finance mechanisms can help mobilize investment, while systemic portfolio implementation environments and local climate investment structures and collaborative implementation environments can support coordinated delivery of investments. Procurement complements financing by creating credible demand conditions that allow new solutions to move from demonstrations and small-scale deployment toward wider commercial adoption.

pathways.title: Locally Anchored Multilevel Climate Finance Structures
pathways.whatItIs: Multilevel climate finance structures can be understood as a range of financing arrangements that help municipalities mobilize and deploy capital for climate and transition investment, in collaboration with other levels of government and the private sector. This could include pooled municipal borrowing facilities, trust funds, special purpose vehicles for projects requiring off-balance sheet financing, blended finance arrangements etc. Their purpose is to create a local mechanism for cities to mobilize and deploy climate finance from diverse sources, including national governments, donors or private financiers.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: In many contexts, the challenge in implementing local climate investments is often not a shortage of capital but matching it to the right portfolio. These finance vehicles and mechanisms can help bridge this gap by connecting portfolios with available capital and can take different forms depending on local government capacity, governance and market conditions.
transferability: Tailor the financing structure to the local fiscal system, borrowing regulations, tax base and market maturity: where decentralization and private-sector depth are stronger, local trust funds or similar vehicles may work well; where responsibilities are devolved but fiscal space is limited, devolved funds may be a better fit; and in more unitary systems, country- or donor-led funds, like the Viability Fund or LoCAL program, may need to be channelled through existing fiscal transfer mechanisms. In context where local governments have creditworthiness, a green bond framework like Lund could be utilized.

When setting up a climate investment fund, start with a focused investment portfolio, aligned with national priorities and plans, so that investor confidence improves and external finance could be mobilized.

Carefully structure SPVs for project financing and implementation. SPVs are legally complex and expensive downscaling to smaller projects requires careful packaging and de-risking for banks and commercial investors to participate.

Regardless of where the fund gets anchored, enable local planning control while bringing in external capital through multilevel partnerships, so finance supports locally defined and locally led climate priorities.
enablingConditions: Credible leadership, commitment and capacities at various levels of government to structure and manage the climate investment vehicles, or access to an intermediary manager, such as Bristol’s Net Zero Investment Co-Innovation Lab or Tamil Nadu’s subnational government, to support local governments in setting up and managing such funds.
Local alignment with national plans, national platforms and coordination with national institutions for long-term sustainability and ownership

Multilevel partnerships with donors, corporates, individuals, DFIs or national governments to mobilize finance or credible intermediary to hold this mandate, manage these partnerships and channel finance to local investment vehicles.

illustrativeExamples.title: Kenya’s County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Kenya’s County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs) demonstrate how devolved climate finance can enable locally led adaptation w...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Kenya’s County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs) demonstrate how devolved climate finance can enable locally led adaptation while remaining anchored in national policy. CCCFs were piloted in Isiolo in 2011–12 and later expanded to Garissa, Kitui, Makueni, Wajir and beyond. These funds identify, prioritize and finance local adaptation investments through county planning and budgeting systems, with county and ward committees steering decisions and local knowledge and climate information built into planning and monitoring. They are designed to blend resources from international climate finance, multilateral development banks, the private sector, national government transfers and county own-source budgets, and several counties have legislated commitments of 1–2 per cent of development budgets to capitalise the fund. This domestic commitment helped attract external finance, including seed funding from the UK and Sweden and a proposal to the Green Climate Fund to expand the model. The model is aligned with Kenya’s National Adaptation Plan (NAP), the National Climate Change Action Plan, and the Climate Change Act. The success of pilots helped pave the way for national scale-up – by 2023 all 47 Kenyan counties had CCCFs in place, creating the basis for a new Financing Locally-Led Climate Action Program funded by the World Bank and the governments of Denmark and Sweden, and led by the National Treasury.

illustrativeExamples.title: LoCAL
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: LoCAL is a country-based mechanism spearheaded by the UN Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) It helps local governments int...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: LoCAL is a country-based mechanism spearheaded by the UN Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) It helps local governments integrate climate adaptation into planning and budgeting through performance-based climate resilience grants and technical and capacity-building support. It channels climate finance to local governments through existing national fiscal transfer systems. In practice, local governments assess risks and needs, prepare adaptation plans, identify and budget priority measures, and implement them through their annual budgeting cycles; performance reviews and audits then inform future allocations. LoCAL is designed to scale in phases, moving from piloting to learning and then to full national roll-out, which makes it a strong example of a multilevel local climate finance structure embedded in national systems. Since 2011, LoCAL has provided USD 8.3 million in grants to 64 local governments, impacting over 5 million people across 12 countries in Asia (Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Lao PDR and Nepal), the Pacific (Tuvalu) and Africa (Benin, Ghana, Mali, Mozambique, Niger and Tanzania).

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Milan for Trees Fund is a locally led trust fund managed by the municipality of Milan and is dedicated to tree planting ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Milan for Trees Fund is a locally led trust fund managed by the municipality of Milan and is dedicated to tree planting in the city. The fund is capitalized through a blend of municipal tax revenues, individual contributions and larger corporate donations. The money is held off the municipal balance sheet, and the fund allows tree planting to extend beyond public land. In 2024, 600 citizens and 36 local business participated to raise over EUR 1.3 million to plant over 4700 trees. It is a good example of how a city can lead local multi-stakeholder partnerships, bringing in private capital to fund place-based climate action. The city of Lund in Sweden is also planning to replicate this model to accelerate municipal tree planting, which will not only improve local climatic conditions but also provide additional economic value to businesses through place-based improvements.

illustrativeExamples.fullText: Tamil Nadu Water and Sanitation Pooled Fund illustrates how a dedicated special purpose vehicle can connect municipal projects with state, national and private finance. Established by the Government of Tamil Nadu as a separate trust, the Fund pooled the borrowing needs of 13 small and medium-sized municipalities and issued a single bond to raise long-term capital for water and sanitation investments. Participating municipalities repaid the Fund through project and local revenues, while the state government strengthened the structure through reserve funds and the ability to intercept fiscal transfers if repayments fell short; a USAID partial guarantee provided additional protection to investors.  By ring-fencing the financing and repayment arrangements, the SPV spread risk, reduced transaction costs and enabled municipalities that could not issue bonds independently to access capital markets. The national government subsequently embedded this approach in its national Pooled Finance Development Fund, through which the central government supports state-level pooled finance entities with project-preparation assistance and credit enhancement. The case shows how national and state governments can establish an intermediary SPV that aggregates local investment needs and mobilizes private capital while municipalities retain responsibility for project delivery and repayment.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Lund’s green bond programme is a strong example of a local climate finance structure because it shows how a city can tra...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Lund’s green bond programme is a strong example of a local climate finance structure because it shows how a city can translate climate priorities into a municipally anchored investment vehicle. Lund began issuing green bonds in 2017, and by end-2025 had an outstanding green bond volume of USD 450 million. Lund municipality updated its green bonds framework, incorporating elements from the EU Taxonomy for sustainable investments, broadening the range of eligible projects. The framework also sets up how projects are selected, monitored and reported, and is used to connect investment planning with climate and sustainability goals while improving transparency and accountability to investors. The portfolio spans climate-smart infrastructure and buildings across the municipality and its wholly owned housing, parking and water utility companies, with examples such as the Lund tramway and the LKF housing project showing how the bond framework channels finance into a tracked green portfolio of approved projects.

pathways.title: Innovative and De-risking Financial Tools and Mechanisms
pathways.whatItIs: De-risking financial tools and mechanisms reduce implementation and investment risk while helping mobilize larger pools of public and private capital. This could include concessional finance, guarantees, insurance and blended-finance mechanisms to crowd in investment, strengthen investor confidence and accelerate delivery of priority climate investments. They work best when linked to strong governance, project portfolios and local investment structures.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Utilizing innovative and de-risking tools and mechanisms is crucial to mitigate perceived high risks and uncertainties for the investors. Many climate investments at the subnational or local level may be held back not by a lack of ambition, institutional arrangements or political momentum behind them, but by the fact that their risks are too high or too uncertain for private investors to engage at scale.
transferability: Match the financial mechanisms and tools to legal and regulatory conditions, capacities of multilevel actors, risk-return profiles of projects and market maturity. Catalytic funding could be most effective in low-capacity contexts that require initial upfront capital to demonstrate implementation capabilities to crowd in additional finance. Insurance and risk pooling are most transferable where climate-disaster exposure is the main challenge to fiscal resilience; local-currency guarantees fit contexts with a bankable portfolio, where the main constraint is credit quality and investor confidence; pooled borrowing works where municipalities already have a shared financing base and want lower-cost market access or have small ticket sizes and limited creditworthiness to access the market individually.

Replication works best when a trusted intermediary can hold the mandate, coordinate actors and manage risk. For example, Viable Cities plays that coordinating role for the Viability fund, linking it with EU grants opportunities, local trust funds, systems demonstrators etc and the wider multilateral initiatives. Similarly, ICLEI and PIDG play the coordinating, implementation or capacity building roles for UIIF and InfraCredit.

Adopt a phased approach for transferability in lower-capacity contexts. UIIFs’ seven-stage roadmap shows that de-risking instruments are more transferable when they are introduced step-by-step, giving cities and parters time to align data, governance and build capacities progressively. Similarly, Viability Fund also plans to adopt a phased approach, focusing on a few high potential projects, cities and partnerships to demonstrate early success and help inspire other actors to replicate the model.

Embed the tools within existing domestic governance systems, portfolios, investors and financial structures. InfraCredit works well when anchored in a sovereign institution and domestic capital markets to mobilize local institutional investors which would benefit from local currency guarantees. Kommuninvest works well because it is owned jointly by municipalities and is tied to their joint guarantees. Viability fund similarly looks to invest in local investment structures from the outset to maximize the impact of its mobilized funds.
enablingConditions: A clear risk profile and a portfolio of investable projects. These tools work best when cities can identify whether the main constraint is credit risk, disaster exposure, foreign exchange risk or early-stage delivery risk, and when there is already a project portfolio that can absorb guarantees, insurance or blended finance.

A legal and regulatory setup that allows the instrument to be deployed. The tools have to align with the regulations for borrowing, guarantees, subsidies, or pooled finance, and public actors need enough budget authority to commit long-term resources to investment portfolios.

Financial structures to absorb capital and integrate innovative financial mechanisms. In contexts where local balance sheets are not strong enough, investment vehicles, like SPVs could be used to integrate mechanisms like aggregation and blended finance.

Risk-bearing capital and counterparties willing to participate. De-risking tools will need first-loss or catalytic capital, a financing partner, and investors prepared to take exposure once risk is reduced. That is visible in KfW/BMZ backing UIIF premiums, and PIDG and NSIA backing InfraCredit to crowd in institutional investors.

The CCFLA Financial Instruments Toolkit is an interactive resource that helps practitioners explore financial instruments for urban climate projects, including how different instruments work and the contexts in which they may be relevant.

It provides structured guidance on navigating the spectrum of urban climate finance instruments—from debt, equity, and guarantees to results-based financing and blended capital structures—helping project developers and municipal leaders match the right financial mechanisms to their specific infrastructure and resilience needs.

illustrativeExamples.title: Viability Fund for Cities
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Viability Fund for Cities is a donor-led, catalytic, multilevel funding platform designed to help cities, especially in ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Viability Fund for Cities is a donor-led, catalytic, multilevel funding platform designed to help cities, especially in EMDEs, to move from isolated projects to scalable, investment-ready climate portfolios by linking local investment vehicles with national, regional and international funders. It is built around local investment funds as a key vehicle for channelling co-finance into city-level priorities. The Fund provides limited catalytic capital to support a small number of “game-changing” interventions and creates a shared framework that can be adapted across contexts, including in the EMDEs. Viability Fund’s theory of change is built around three components – align funders across public and private sectors, co-finance priority investments that no single actor would back alone, and aggregate demand through procurement so that demonstrated solutions can move into wider deployment. The Fund aims to partner with key global funders and implementation actors to deploy EUR 10 million by 2030 in co-financing and another EUR 10 million in aggregated demand through a focus on climate-aligned procurement.

subExamples.title: Viability Fund’s support offer
subExamples.excerpt: The Viability Fund offers cities two core forms of support. First, catalytic co-financing: through i...
subExamples.fullText:
The Viability Fund offers cities two core forms of support. First, catalytic co-financing: through its Co-finance pillar, the Fund will contribute roughly 10 percent of the capital needed for a local investment, taking an early, credibility-anchoring position that is then topped up through national and international co-financing dialogues rather than covering the full cost itself. Second, a local investment fund as a service: because a city must establish its own local climate investment fund, built on shared principles, to receive the Fund's co-financing, the Fund helps set up and run that vehicle, potentially through a fund-manager partner, so it can channel capital to local stakeholders such as solar, batteries, energy infrastructure and SMEs, and recycle returns into harder-to-finance areas like wetlands. Alongside both sits governance and coordination support: aligning funders around common grant principles without pooling capital, and helping cities connect governance, investment planning and procurement — reflecting the Fund's guiding logic that finance follows governance.

To know more about with the Viability Fund for cities, click here.

illustrativeExamples.title: Kommuninvest
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Kommuninvest is a locally led Swedish municipal aggregation mechanism that pools borrowing demand from municipalities an...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Kommuninvest is a locally led Swedish municipal aggregation mechanism that pools borrowing demand from municipalities and regions, giving them access to capital on more favourable terms. It raises money in the market and on-lends it to its members, operating as a lending-only institution rather than a grant fund or equity vehicle. The model is backed by a joint guarantee from its 282 municipal and 15 regional members, which helps de-risk lending and lower borrowing costs. In 2025, Kommuninvest’s total lending reached SEK 563.9 billion, showing the scale that pooled municipal finance can achieve.

To know more about Kommuninvest, click here.

illustrativeExamples.title: Urban Infrastructure Insurance Facility (UIIF)
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Urban Infrastructure Insurance Facility (UIIF) is a multilevel insurance-based risk pooling mechanism involving municipa...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Urban Infrastructure Insurance Facility (UIIF) is a multilevel insurance-based risk pooling mechanism involving municipal governments, international donor agencies and city networks. It demonstrates how cities can address climate and disaster exposure risks and protect critical infrastructure. In the UIIF model, ten cities in Latin America and the Caribbean undergo risk assessments that inform tailored insurance coverage and disaster risk reduction measures, with individual city risks transferred into a pooled structure that reduces premiums through economies of scale and risk sharing. After a disaster, cities can access financing more quickly to rebuild infrastructure and support vulnerable residents, while also benefiting from better risk management, legal and technical support, and stronger relationships with financial institutions. UIIF follows a 7-stage roadmap, which includes profiling and selecting cities, assessing risk and tailoring products, designing premium subsidies, tendering the insurance solution, and disbursing the subsidy over time.

To know more about UIIF, click here.

illustrativeExamples.title: InfraCredit Nigeria
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: InfraCredit Nigeria is a strong example of how a local credit-enhancement facility can unlock domestic capital for infra...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
InfraCredit Nigeria is a strong example of how a local credit-enhancement facility can unlock domestic capital for infrastructure. Established in 2017 through a partnership between PIDG, GuarantCo and the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, InfraCredit provides NGN-denominated guarantees that improve the credit quality of local-currency debt instruments and help projects access longer-tenor finance from institutional investors such as pension funds, insurers and banks that would otherwise not invest. By end-2024, it had guaranteed 24 transactions mobilising over NGN 200 billion in private investment, supported nearly NGN 150 billion in bond issuances, and helped first-time issuers such as North South Power access the domestic capital market. InfraCredit’s portfolio spans projects in Abuja, Lagos, Ondo, Imo, Abia, Cross River, Enugu, Bayelsa, Ado Ekiti and Victoria Island, including solar mini-grids, embedded power, housing, telecoms, a ring road and industrial infrastructure, showing how a national credit-enhancement vehicle can channel finance into a wide range of place-based investments.

The model has also been replicated beyond Nigeria through sister facilities in Pakistan, Kenya and Cambodia, with additional markets including Vietnam, Ghana and Francophone West Africa under development or review.

To know more about InfraCredit Nigeria, click here.

conceptBoxes.title: What is Blended Finance?
conceptBoxes.excerpt: Blended finance is the strategic use of catalytic concessional public or philanthropic capital to mobilize and de-risk additional commercial private capital for sustainable development and climate goals.
conceptBoxes.fullText: Blended finance is the strategic use of a limited amount of concessional public or philanthropic capital to mobilize additional finance, primarily from commercial and private sources — toward sustainable development and climate goals. Rather than a single financial instrument, it is a structuring approach: public actors (donors, development agencies, philanthropies, and development finance institutions) absorb or share risks that would otherwise deter private investors, improving a project's risk-return profile enough to attract market-rate capital. The concessional capital at the core of a blended structure can take several forms, including grants, concessional debt or equity, guarantees, and other risk-sharing facilities. These de-risking mechanisms matter most in emerging markets and developing economies, where country-specific risk accounts for between 60 and 90 percent of investors' risk considerations, and where about 80–90 percent of climate mitigation investment is expected to come from the private sector. The overarching goal is to crowd in private money that would not have been invested otherwise, deploying only as much public subsidy as is needed to make a project viable.

pathways.title: Collaborative Portfolio Implementation Environments
pathways.whatItIs: A collaborative portfolio implementation environment is a place-based setup where public, private and civic actors jointly implement, test and adapt a portfolio of mutually reinforcing interventions around a shared transition mission. These place-based initiatives go beyond individual pilots or project-level coordination activities. Instead, they create a shared, ongoing environment where governance, finance, procurement, regulations, organizational cultures and technologies are aligned around a common mission, such as climate action. These implementation environments help generate the evidence, partnerships and institutional changes needed to move successful interventions toward investment and scale.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Developing a portfolio and the governance and finance arrangements around it is not sufficient on its own; climate portfolios also need collaborative implementation environments where public, private and civic actors can jointly contribute, deliver, learn and adapt. Without that environment, portfolios can fragment into isolated projects, learning is harder to share, and the system conditions needed for scale do not change.
transferability: Transfer the core functions of implementation environments, while keeping the institutional form adaptable. The transferable core is a defined local system or place, a shared mission, system mapping, a portfolio approach, continuous orchestration, learning and pathways to finance and scale. The institution leading these functions should reflect the governance context.

Keep implementation locally grounded. Deep transition challenges cannot be solved by externally assembled consortia alone. Local actors with knowledge, mandate, relationships and implementation capacity should anchor the process, while external partners add specialist capabilities. The examples cited above defined their own local priorities, i.e., decarbonization in Lund, land aggregation in Bristol or project preparation for low-carbon building retrofits in Central Asia.

Embed implementation in the institution best placed to provide political mandate, coordination and continuity. Where local governments have sufficient autonomy and capacity (e.g., system demonstrators in Lund, Bristol and Bogota), they can anchor the process directly; where they do not, national ministries, international agencies or other intermediaries (i.e., CCFLA for Local Hubs or a national agency, NIUA, in CITIIS 2.0) can provide the convening power and long-term ownership needed to sustain implementation and scale.

Funding and participation arrangements should fit the governance and institutional context. Whether participating members in a portfolio implementation environment have funded roles, in-kind contributions or voluntary commitments will vary by fiscal capacities, partnership needs and the enabling environments – what matters is that the model is strong enough to sustain engagement and keep the implementation environment moving. For example, the Swedish system demonstrators funded all consortium partners while the local hubs engaged stakeholders without direct funding.

Phase the implementation based on system readiness. In contexts with low readiness levels, implementation should focus on diagnostics, convening, mapping and coalition building (e.g., Central Asia Hub). As readiness increases, focus should shift towards investment planning, testbed selection and portfolio development (see Action 4 for guidance on these). Full implementation should be financed once the mission is co-owned, the coordination function is in place, stakeholders are mobilized, barriers are known and a portfolio is in place.

Use clear, accessible language and simplify the methodology where necessary. The Swedish experience showed that even relatively mature cities struggled when system-demonstrator concepts became overly abstract or innovation-heavy. In lower-capacity contexts especially, guidance should focus on practical functions and outputs rather than specialist transition terminology.

Connect local implementation to national systems from the beginning. Demonstrators are more likely to scale when local evidence can inform national policy, funding programmes, investment priorities and future climate plans. Some System Demonstrators, e.g., in Uganda, have demonstrated that weak national-local institutional connections can constrain scaling even when local demonstration is successful.

Build in a pathway from implementation to scale from the outset. The model is more transferable when it linked from the outset to investment, procurement and replication routes. These pathways may involve national governments, DFIs, PPFs or international donors, depending on the funding context and portfolio readiness. For example, EnergyNet is expected to scale through the Viability Fund, Bristol scaled via the UK Small Sites Aggregator, and Central Asia Hub is expected to scale through project preparation pathways involving Gap Fund, FELICITY II, and financing pathways involving GCF and EIB.
enablingConditions: A political mandate and co-owned decision making between public and private actors.
A dedicated coordination function or intermediary capable of holding the implementation environment together, capture learnings iteratively and
Reliable local data, evidence and a testbed (e.g., a city) so that baseline data and observed barriers could inform implementation.
Flexible and sustained funding for implementation and learning, including resources for orchestration and experimentation, not only capital expenditure on individual assets.

A multilevel pathway for policy and institutional learning, allowing barriers identified in the testbed to be escalated to the regional or national levels and successful approaches to feed into future plans, policies and investment frameworks.
Credible pathways to connect bankable portfolios to finance providers and market-shaping actors, including governments, private developers, investors DFIs and procurement actors.

implementationGuidance.title: The below actions could help create collaborative portfolio environments.
implementationGuidance.content: The below actions could help create collaborative portfolio environments.

implementationGuidance.title: Anchor implementation in a locally relevant mission and system boundary
implementationGuidance.content: Connect it to the city’s climate/investment priorities and, where possible, national climate priorities, rather than starting with a technology or individual project.

implementationGuidance.title: Map the system, actors, structural barriers and opportunities before selecting solutions
implementationGuidance.content: This is important because the system demonstrator experience showed that starting with existing solutions often reproduces incremental pilots rather than creating space for more transformative approaches.

implementationGuidance.title: Start with a real local testbed where the portfolio can...
implementationGuidance.content: Start with a real local testbed where the portfolio can be implemented against actual users, assets and constraints. It should be bounded enough to manage but expansive enough to generate evidence for scale and expose the governance, infrastructure or market challenges to overcome.

implementationGuidance.title: Convene the delivery ecosystem and keep it aligned through continuous orchestration
implementationGuidance.content: While local governments could anchor the portfolio implementation process, it also needs higher tiers of governments, utilities, property owners, developers, investors and community actors, with continuous dialogue and coordination to maintain momentum and identify key implementation challenges. A dedicated orchestration function is also needed to maintain alignment across the portfolio, bring in relevant actors as implementation needs evolve, resolve bottlenecks, capture learning and sustain momentum toward the shared mission.

implementationGuidance.title: Implement the portfolio as one coherent system of mutually reinforcing...
implementationGuidance.content: Implement the portfolio as one coherent system of mutually reinforcing intervention, not a set of separate projects. The portfolio should connect governance, finance, procurement, regulation, behaviour and technology so that the combined effect shifts the system, not just individual parts of it. Not every intervention needs to be commercially investible; the portfolio can generate investible pipelines as learning progresses.

implementationGuidance.title: Use implementation to generate evidence that “de-risks” policy and investment and enables scale-up
implementationGuidance.content: Track what changes in regulation, costs, technical performance, institutional arrangements, behaviour and business models—not simply whether an individual technology works.

illustrativeExamples.title: CITIIS 2.0 (City Investments to Innovate, Integrate and Sustain) in India
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: CITIIS 2.0 (City Investments to Innovate, Integrate and Sustain) in India shows how a national programme can create a co...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
CITIIS 2.0 (City Investments to Innovate, Integrate and Sustain) in India shows how a national programme can create a collaborative portfolio environment that helps cities to implement their climate-related project portfolios. Conceived by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs with the French Development Agency, KfW, the European Union and the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), the programme supports up to 18 competitively selected city projects focused on circular economy and integrated waste management, while also backing state-level climate action and national-level institutional strengthening. The programme is coordinated through a PMU at NIUA, which the operational guidelines say is responsible for overall management and support on project management, environmental and social safeguards, monitoring and evaluation, knowledge capitalisation, and communications and outreach. Selected cities are supported by domestic experts and a pool of international mentors and transversal experts, with domestic experts providing day-to-day assistance and regular on-site missions. Governance of CITIIS is reinforced through a jury and an Apex Committee for final selection and periodic review, helping connect funding decisions to delivery capacity and accountability.

Click here to know more about CITIIS.
