illustrativeExamples.title: System Demonstrators
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: System Demonstrators provide implementation environments that put investible portfolios into on-ground local testbeds wh...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: System Demonstrators provide implementation environments that put investible portfolios into on-ground local testbeds where public, private and civic actors jointly shape the implementation, exchange learnings and adapt as needed. Rather than a project-by-project implementation approach, the demonstrators create a systemic implementation environment around a shared mission and a coordinated portfolio of investments, with continuous orchestration around governance, finance, procurement, infrastructure, regulations, behaviors and technology. Key examples of System Demonstrator implementation are highlighted below:

subExamples.title: CoAction Lund
subExamples.excerpt: CoAction Lund shows how a city-led system demonstrator can orchestrate a complex implementation ecosystem around a share...
subExamples.fullText:
CoAction Lund shows how a city-led system demonstrator can orchestrate a complex implementation ecosystem around a shared mission of climate neutrality by 2030. In Brunnshög, the municipality brought together infrastructure providers, employers, property owners, universities and solution providers to deliver more than 40 coordinated activities across mobility and energy, with funding kept flexible so that resources can shift toward the most promising models as learning emerges. One major “game changer” is EnergyNet, a decentralised local electricity network that enables buildings, vehicles and local energy resources to share renewable electricity.  By testing EnergyNet on ground, CoAction Lund has surfaced regulatory and market barriers around grid codes, data-sharing and local markets, helping inform the adjustments needed for scale and mainstream distributed energy systems in cities facing increasing electrification demands and grid constraints. Finally, a shared evaluation plan, based on agreed indicators, tracks both activities and system‑level outcomes, feeding into regular reflection and learning cycles. EnergyNet’s successful demonstration has led to the Viability Fund for Cities identifying its expansion to other cities as a key investment opportunity,

To know more about CoAction Lund, click here. To know more about EnergyNet, click here.

subExamples.title: Green Routes, Bogotá
subExamples.excerpt: Green Routes, Bogotá demonstrates how a system demonstrator can build a collaborative implementation environment around ...
subExamples.fullText: Green Routes, Bogotá demonstrates how a system demonstrator can build a collaborative implementation environment around a shared evidence base. In Bogotá, the challenge was to coordinate thousands of freight operators in a citywide logistics system, so the demonstrator brought freight operators, shippers and public agencies together through the Urban Logistics Network, led by the city’s Secretariat of Mobility and working with the Secretariat of Environment. As part of the implementation, Green Routes, a consortium of four technology companies, developed a real-time routing platform, which is part of an interconnected portfolio or related actions, including emissions labelling, circulation rules, loading and unloading investments, sustainable driving guidelines and a proposed district freight fund. The platform’s key contribution is the negotiated data-sharing arrangement, which would give the city the evidence it needs to plan freight more effectively, while also helping operators optimise routes and costs. The next steps for this systems demonstrator are to develop business models and sustainable revenue streams. Click here to know more about Green Routes.

subExamples.title: Makindye Ssabagabo’s Green Community Cities demonstrator
subExamples.excerpt: Makindye Ssabagabo’s Green Community Cities demonstrator brings together the municipality, UN-Habitat, Viable Cities and...
subExamples.fullText: Makindye Ssabagabo’s Green Community Cities demonstrator brings together the municipality, UN-Habitat, Viable Cities and an international consortium working across urban planning, low-carbon construction, recycled building materials, organic-waste processing, water systems and finance to address affordable housing as a wider urban system. The model combined modular and incremental housing, circular-economy enterprises, renewable energy, water-saving technologies, skills development and local employment, supported through a proposed blend of grants, concessional capital, private investment, microfinance and cross-subsidisation between market-rate and affordable housing. Experience from the Climate Smart Cities Challenge also surfaced an important implementation challenge – internationally assembled solution teams were more effective where they were strongly anchored in local actors and institutions, and that weaker local collaboration and national-local connections made implementation and scaling more difficult in cases such as Makindye than in more institutionally mature settings. The example therefore shows both the value of bringing diverse capabilities into a shared implementation portfolio and the importance of ensuring that orchestration is rooted in institutions with sufficient local mandate, relationships and capacity.

subExamples.title: Bristol Thriving Places
subExamples.excerpt: Bristol Thriving Places demonstrates how a system demonstrator can overcome a regulatory bottleneck into to implement in...
subExamples.fullText:
Bristol Thriving Places demonstrates how a system demonstrator can overcome a regulatory bottleneck into to implement infrastructure and scale through multilevel collaboration, including with the national government. In Bristol, the challenge was affordable, zero-carbon housing on small brownfield sites that conventional development treated as unviable; the city, working through Bristol City Council and the Bristol Housing Festival, convened a consortium led by social housing developer EDAROTH, together with housing associations, regeneration developer Igloo, energy, and digital infrastructure providers, government agencies, a private ‘gov-tech’ firm and research partners to deliver a portfolio of net-zero social homes, a multi-capital value toolkit, a policy and regulation discovery stream and a digital twin. The demonstrator’s key move was site aggregation: by treating many small council-owned sites as one programme, Bristol created the scale needed for delivery, prompted the council to review its treasury strategy to enable programme-level appraisal, and secured a development agreement of around £10 million through an existing national procurement framework. The model then fed into the UK government’s Small Sites Aggregator, a national programme launched by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government with private and public partners and an ambition of enabling 10,000 social rent homes a year.

Click here to know more about Bristol Thriving Places

subExamples.title: Stockholm’s STOLT system demonstrator
subExamples.excerpt: Stockholm’s STOLT system demonstrator is advancing the city’s ambition for an emission-free inner city by 2030 by using ...
subExamples.fullText: Stockholm’s STOLT system demonstrator is advancing the city’s ambition for an emission-free inner city by 2030 by using the introduction of a Class 3 Environmental Zone and the Urban Environment Zone in Gamla Stan as strategic windows of opportunity for wider transport-system transformation. Rather than testing a single solution, STOLT coordinates a broad ecosystem of city departments, businesses, research and innovation actors, infrastructure stakeholders and civil society around a portfolio that includes stakeholder dialogue, fossil-free transport procurement, electrified construction, off-peak logistics and emerging concepts such as co-loading hubs. This coordination is particularly significant in Stockholm’s complex institutional setting – the demonstrator has succeeded in working across municipal departments and external stakeholders through recurring coordination, shared portfolio oversight and continuous adaptation. pathways.title: Aggregated Procurement as a Market-Shaping and Industrial Transition Mechanism
pathways.whatItIs: Aggregated and pooled procurement are a market-shaping and industrial transition mechanisms in which cities, alongside subnational and national agencies and other public and private buyers coordinate purchasing power to create a stronger, aggregated demand for low-carbon and resilience-enhancing goods, services and infrastructure. The market signal can be strengthened further if local procurement activities are aligned with national climate priorities. In this pathway, aggregation can mean multiple buyers coordinating demand while keeping separate budgets and contracts, while pooled procurement combines demand into a single fund or joint tender. The mechanism can operate within a city, across municipalities, or vertically across city, state and national levels.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Subnational governments collectively spend over USD 6 trillion a year on goods and services – roughly 8% of global GDP – yet this leverage is fragmented across departments and not coordinated with private demand, so markets receive no stable signal to invest in low-carbon materials. Procurement, when used strategically to align with climate outcomes, can help create a unified, more stable demand for green and resilient infrastructure.
transferability: Use the procurement model that fits the capacity and governance context. This may be a trust fund with built-in governance, a nationally coordinated tender, or a city-level mandate; the transferable core is the combination of political mandate, technical support, and clear criteria for aggregating demand.

Choose an appropriate procurement jurisdiction based on capacities and governance arrangements. Where cities have strong procurement authority and large infrastructure pipelines, intra-city aggregation can shape markets within one jurisdiction. Where capacities or enabling conditions are weaker at the municipal level, pooling between cities can work, but it usually needs a national intermediary or coordinator to standardize and hold the process together, as in RAMCC and India’s Grand Challenge.

Adapt the procurement objectives based on national climate priorities. For example, cities can focus on procurement models for low-carbon construction materials or e-buses where national priorities include renewable energy and decarbonization, so the market signal reinforces the wider policy direction.
enablingConditions: Clear procurement authority to set procurement rules, define award criteria and, where relevant, coordinate across departments or buyers.
Multilevel coordination capabilities, especially with higher levels of government and the private actors to implement the procurement models
Enabling regulations, procurement frameworks and financing or technical support at the national and subnational levels
Technical capacity within subnational or local governments to design, evaluate and monitor climate-aligned tenders
Early and continuous market engagement to assess readiness of suppliers, manufacturers and other industry actors.

illustrativeExamples.title: Intra-city aggregated procurement in Zurich
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Intra-city aggregated procurement in Zurich demonstrates how a city government can leverage its regulatory mandates and ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
Intra-city aggregated procurement in Zurich demonstrates how a city government can leverage its regulatory mandates and purchasing power to aggregate demand from public and private sectors within its jurisdiction and create a market for low-carbon infrastructure. In 2002, the city began with a pilot showing that a new school could use 80 percent recycled aggregates in concrete, then introduced a 25 percent minimum requirement for recycled aggregates in concrete for new public buildings in 2005 and later tightened its procurement in 2013 to require low-carbon cement as well. Over time, this public procurement approach, together with revisions to Swiss standards and active engagement with local producers, helped create a local market for recycled concrete that later spread into the private sector. As a result, 90% of public concrete used in the city is now recycled (up to 50% recycled aggregates), and between 2016-21, the city’s concrete-related CO₂ emissions were reduced by 25–30% (7,430 tonnes CO₂ emissions saved). Zurich’s procurement policy succeeded in creating a market for recycled concrete that was later spread to the private market, helping aggregate the city-wide demand towards low-emissions infrastructure.

illustrativeExamples.title: The Grand Challenge, India
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: The Grand Challenge, India is an example of a vertically coordinated (i.e., between multiple levels of government) poole...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
The Grand Challenge, India is an example of a vertically coordinated (i.e., between multiple levels of government) pooled procurement model for urban green transport – a capital-intensive sector. The model aimed to scale up the deployment of e-buses in India and support the transition to low-emissions fleets. Led by Convergence Energy Service Limited (CESL) under the Ministry of Power, and supported by TUMI E-bus Mission, the model pooled demand from multiple cities for e-buses, reduced transaction costs through a single tendering process and used subsidies from the national government, with some state contributions as well. CESL first invited cities to estimate demand and share route, depot and charging information, then consolidated those inputs into a standardized pooled tender. Before issuing the procurement, CESL also consulted OEMs through informal discussions and an initial expression of interest, which helped it test market appetite and adjust the tender design. The tender was then split into five lots with different technical specifications, and bids were selected based on the lowest cost per kilometre. The model relied on a gross cost contract and a mobility-as-a-service structure where private operators own and run the e-buses and charging infrastructure for 12 years, after which they transfer the assets to cities. This helped shift the upfront costs away from cities and suppliers while helping scale a new market for electric buses.

Click here to know more about the Grand Challenge.

illustrativeExamples.excerpt: RAMCC Trust Fund, Argentina demonstrates how a horizontally coordinated pooled procurement vehicles, coordinated horizon...
illustrativeExamples.fullText:
RAMCC Trust Fund, Argentina demonstrates how a horizontally coordinated pooled procurement vehicles, coordinated horizontally (i.e., between local governments), can consolidate a fragmented municipal demand into a strong market signal. RAMCC is a coalition of 270 municipalities, and the Trust Fund, established by RAMCC in 2018, helps participating municipalities to finance and deliver projects in their climate action plan by procuring suited climate-smart technologies at lower costs. Each participating municipality is a Trustee and is represented by its mayor in the Assembly of Mayors – a forum for Trustees to set out their project implementation priorities and share progress. The Assembly also elects the executive committee, the Mayor City Council, comprising a group of 5 mayors (one president and four vice presidents), which provides strategic oversight for the Trust’s financing activities each year. A third body, the Executive Secretariat, provides Trustees with technical support to develop climate plans, undertake technical studies, and develop financing proposals. Municipalities approve budgets, pool and allocate funds. The Mayor City Council issues pooled tenders, award contracts and pays technology suppliers. The Trust Fund has initially focused on LED lighting procurement, achieving economies of scale and financial savings and delivering measurable emissions, energy savings.

countryJourneys.tagline: An Evolving Mission-Oriented Approach to Urban Climate Transition
countryJourneys.summary: Showcasing how Viable Cities, Climate City Contract 2030, the Coordination Function, and System Demonstrators form an interconnected multilevel delivery system spanning 48 municipalities and 6 national agencies.
countryJourneys.headerTitle: Sweden’s Multilevel Governance and Implementation Journey
countryJourneys.headerDescription: An in-depth analysis of Sweden’s evolving mission-oriented innovation ecosystem, demonstrating how municipal autonomy, recurring political contracts, system demonstrators, and emerging local investment structures connect into a continuous multilevel delivery architecture.
countryJourneys.tabASubtitle: An Evolving Mission-Oriented Approach to Urban Climate Transition
countryJourneys.premisesHeading: Two Central Premises of Sweden’s Multilevel Journey
countryJourneys.premisesIntro: Sweden’s approach to urban climate transformation is grounded in two fundamental institutional premises:

premises.title: No Single Actor Delivers Alone
premises.description: No individual institution or level of government possesses all mandates, assets, or capital required for complete urban decarbonization.

premises.title: Finance Follows Governance
premises.description: Capital and financing instruments become dramatically more effective when the governance, coordination, and portfolio structuring needed to organize collective action are firmly in place.

contextSections.title: An Evolving, Iterative Governance Architecture
paragraphs: Sweden’s multilevel climate governance model has evolved iteratively, as successive stages of climate action exposed new governance, delivery and financing challenges and opportunities. This evolution has been shaped by strong municipal autonomy, a well-developed research and innovation system, established municipal financing capacity and a governance culture that supports experimentation and learning across institutional boundaries.

contextSections.title: Municipalities as a "Gathering Force"
paragraphs: Swedish municipalities have substantial responsibility for systems central to climate transition, including spatial planning, infrastructure, municipal companies, procurement and investment. Yet many regulatory, financial and infrastructure conditions are determined nationally or at European level, while businesses, utilities, property owners and citizens control important assets and decisions.

Municipalities can instead act as a **“gathering force”**, connecting their own mandates with actors whose decisions are also necessary for transition. This has encouraged a shift from traditional municipal governance toward more network-based, multilevel forms of governance and coordination.

contextSections.title: Viable Cities: A National Platform Orchestrating the Swedish Ecosystem
paragraphs: Sweden's multilevel model developed through its mission-oriented innovation ecosystem. **Viable Cities** was established in 2017 and progressively brought municipalities, national agencies, research institutions, businesses and civil society around the mission of climate-neutral cities by 2030.
Rather than attempting national scale immediately, the programme developed approaches with pioneer municipalities:

bulletPoints.label: 48 Municipalities
bulletPoints.text: in 2024 (representing approximately half of Sweden's total population)

contextSections.title: Integrating into Ordinary Planning Cycles (Climate City Contract 2030)
paragraphs: As participation grew, experience demonstrated that a shared mission needed to be translated into durable political commitments, locally owned transition processes and continuous national–local coordination. **Climate City Contract 2030** along with **Transition Arenas** and later **Samordningsfunktionen (the Coordination Function)** developed within this context.

Importantly, the emerging governance process was designed to interact directly with municipalities' ordinary planning, budgeting and political cycles and to be reviewed and renewed annually, rather than becoming a parallel climate-governance structure. The process has also helped national agencies identify how their programmes, policy instruments and funding calls can be better coordinated with municipal implementation needs and with one another.

contextSections.title: Shifting from Isolated Pilots to System Demonstrators
paragraphs: A second challenge emerged from Sweden's experience with innovation and pilots. Individual technologies or projects could succeed technically without scaling because surrounding governance, regulation, infrastructure, business models, finance, procurement or behaviours remained unchanged.

This shifted attention from testing individual solutions toward changing the systems in which solutions must operate. **System Demonstrators**, including those in Lund and Stockholm, emerged as a way to bring multiple actors and interventions together around bounded real-world transition challenges and progressively connect experimentation with cities' wider transition portfolios.

contextSections.title: Bridging the Financing Gap: Local Climate Investment Structures & Viability Fund
paragraphs: As these governance and delivery approaches matured, they exposed a further gap between transition priorities and investment. Urban transition portfolios can involve multiple owners, different risk and maturity profiles and enabling interventions that are not themselves investable. Sweden already has strong municipal borrowing capacity through **Kommuninvest**, but conventional debt does not by itself provide project preparation, portfolio structuring, catalytic capital or coordination across actors and assets.

This has led to emerging work on **Local Climate Investment Structures**, including learning from the **EnergyNet** use case, to better connect locally owned transition priorities with investment and finance.

This thinking has informed the emerging **Viability Fund for Cities**, intended to strengthen connections between systemic urban transformation, local investment and national and international finance. In parallel, work on aggregated demand and market shaping, including **First Mover Cities**, reflects recognition that finance alone is insufficient for scale: cities and other urban actors can also use coordinated purchasing and credible demand signals to help create markets for transition solutions.

actions.title: Develop Shared Commitments, Political Alignment and Ownership
paragraphs: **Climate City Contract 2030** provides the recurring process through which municipalities, national agencies and Viable Cities establish shared direction and commitments. The contracts are voluntary rather than legally binding and are renewed through successive cycles of review, learning and political recommitment. Municipalities retain locally adapted pathways, while national agencies and Viable Cities make complementary commitments around enabling conditions, coordination and support.

At local level, **Transition Arenas** extend ownership of climate action beyond municipal government, bringing public, private, academic and civic actors together to co-create transition priorities and portfolios. More recently, **Joint Commitments** have enabled groups of municipalities to work collectively on recurring challenges—including governance, climate investment and procurement—rather than addressing them city by city.
actions.enabledSummary: Sweden has expanded the initiative from nine municipalities in 2019 to 48 municipalities, representing approximately half the country's population, while retaining locally owned transition processes. The opportunity is to embed commitments into ordinary political, planning, budgeting and investment processes so they endure beyond programme and political cycles.

actions.title: Develop Enabling Environments
paragraphs: Sweden's approach illustrates a continuous process of assessing enabling-environments. Climate City Contracts and Transition Arenas have surfaced implementation barriers and needs, while the Coordination Function identifies recurring governance gaps across municipalities.

**System Demonstrators** deepen this diagnostic function through real-world implementation. They examine key barriers and transformation potential across governance, regulation, finance and business models, infrastructure, behaviour and technology, allowing cities and partners to understand not only whether an intervention works but what surrounding conditions must change for systemic transformation to occur.
actions.enabledSummary: Barriers identified through local experience can become inputs into subsequent portfolios, coordination and policy discussions. The opportunity is converting dispersed implementation evidence into sufficiently systematic information that national actors can act upon.

actions.title: Institutionalize Multilevel Governance Frameworks and National Platforms
paragraphs: **Viable Cities** provides the national platform and intermediary infrastructure connecting municipalities, national agencies and wider transition actors. Rather than acting simply as another programme participant, it provides continuity across the different governance and implementation functions of the Swedish model.

Within the platform, the **Coordination Function (Samordningsfunktionen)** provides dedicated intermediary capacity for analysis, facilitation, coordination and learning. It helps identify recurring municipal needs and governance gaps, supports interaction between municipalities and national agencies, and feeds experience into subsequent Climate City Contract cycles. The six participating national agencies also use joint action planning to connect their commitments with their mandates, programmes and policy instruments.
actions.enabledSummary: The combination of a national platform, recurring governance process and intermediary function creates a route for local experience to inform national coordination and for national developments to connect back to cities. The opportunity is sustaining this intermediary capacity and strengthening how implementation evidence translates into adjustments in national support.

actions.title: Jointly Prioritize, Plan and Prepare Investment Portfolios
paragraphs: Climate City Contracts help translate shared commitments into locally owned transition priorities. Through Transition Arenas and related planning processes, municipalities and their partners organize these priorities into transition portfolios, which include interconnected actions spanning investment, policy, governance, procurement and capacity. As these portfolios mature, cities can identify their investment needs and develop investment plans for the components requiring finance. This process is still at different stages across participating municipalities, so not all Swedish cities yet have mature investment plans.

Transition portfolios also provide the strategic basis for **System Demonstrators**. While Climate City Contracts address the municipality's wider transition, System Demonstrators focus on more bounded systemic challenges and are increasingly grounded in cities' Climate City Contract priorities and portfolios. This helps ensure that demonstration activity contributes to the wider transition rather than operating as a standalone pilot.

caseStudy.title: Case: EnergyNet’s Portfolio Approach
paragraphs: EnergyNet shows why transition priorities need to be organized as portfolios rather than standalone projects. Emerging as a “game-changer” intervention through CoAction Lund's work on local energy systems, EnergyNet is a decentralized local electricity network architecture that enables buildings, vehicles and local energy resources to share renewable electricity, reducing dependence on conventional grid reinforcement.

Its implementation is connected to a wider set of interventions across buildings, energy infrastructure, mobility and multiple public and private actors. The portfolio approach helps identify these interdependencies and the combination of actions needed to enable the transition, while also surfacing investment needs and barriers for further preparation.

actions.enabledSummary: Sweden has progressively connected shared political commitments with locally anchored portfolios and investment needs, creating a clearer bridge between climate governance and investment planning. The opportunity is to strengthen investment planning and preparation across municipalities with different levels of capacity and maturity, while retaining the broader systemic interventions needed to deliver the transition.

actions.title: Mobilize Finance, Shape Local Markets and Deliver Investment Portfolios
paragraphs: The transition portfolios developed under Climate City Contracts contain different types of interventions and therefore require different pathways to implementation and scale. Sweden is increasingly connecting three such functions: **systemic implementation through System Demonstrators**, **preparation and financing through emerging Local Climate Investment Structures**, and **aggregated demand and market shaping through initiatives such as First Mover Cities**.

Sweden's experience shows that while debt financing through Kommuninvest is well established for creditworthy municipal investments, systemic transitions require complementary financing and implementation tools. **Local Climate Investment Structures** are being developed to bridge transition portfolios and finance, helping cities and partners package multi-asset interventions, structure investment vehicles, combine public and private capital and aggregate smaller projects into investable scale.

To connect these local structures with larger pools of capital, the **Viability Fund for Cities** is being developed as an institutional intermediary connecting cities with national and international public and private capital. It is intended to perform three core functions:

1. **Align**: Channel and coordinate multiple sources of capital around locally owned transition portfolios.
2. **Co-finance**: Deploy concessional, catalytic and risk-bearing capital to unlock private and commercial investment.
3. **Demand**: Support aggregated demand, procurement and pipeline preparation across cities.

In parallel, **First Mover Cities** illustrates how Swedish municipalities can use collective market-shaping and procurement demand—in heavy transport, construction and energy—to accelerate market readiness for zero-emission solutions, showing that finance and demand aggregation must work together to scale transition solutions.

caseStudy.title: Case: Local Climate Investment Frameworks (EnergyNet Use Case)
paragraphs: **EnergyNet** shows how systemic implementation can generate investment needs that cannot be organized as a single project. Scaling local energy systems requires coordinated investment across buildings, utilities, grids, storage and mobility, involving multiple public and private owners. Costs, revenues and resilience benefits accrue to different actors, while investments have different maturity, risk and return profiles. Some investments may be able to access conventional finance, while others require preparation, guarantees or catalytic capital.

This is the need Local Climate Investment Structures are intended to address. In Sweden, these structures are being developed to organize and finance interconnected investments spanning multiple owners, assets and financing needs. EnergyNet is being used as a practical case to develop this emerging approach, including how investments can be prepared, coordinated and matched with appropriate capital.

While EnergyNet is a use case for the Swedish local climate investment approach, the underlying functions – i.e., coordinating multiple actors and assets, preparing investments and matching different financing needs with appropriate sources of capital – can be adapted to other sectors and contexts. For example, locally anchored water funds in Quito, Bogotá and Nairobi illustrate different institutional approaches to coordinating stakeholders and finance around shared water-system priorities.

actions.enabledSummary: Sweden is moving from individual municipal finance approaches toward structured interfaces between transition portfolios, local investment vehicles, national and international finance and market-shaping mechanisms. The opportunity is to operationalize these financing structures and prove their ability to crowd in private capital at scale.

actions.title: Monitor Progress, Facilitate Learning and Adapt Joint Strategies
paragraphs: Climate City Contracts provide the primary framework for recurring review, learning and adaptation. Annual revisions allow municipalities and national agencies to review progress, update transition priorities and portfolios, and adjust commitments based on experience.

The national platform supports horizontal learning across the 48 participating municipalities through peer exchange, shared development and joint commitments, while the Coordination Function identifies recurring implementation challenges and feeds them into national coordination and policy discussions.

**System Demonstrators** function as real-world learning environments that test not only technical solutions but also regulatory, governance and financial conditions. Evidence generated through demonstrators can directly inform subsequent iterations of Climate City Contracts and policy dialogue, creating a feedback loop between local experimentation, citywide portfolios and national enabling conditions.
actions.enabledSummary: Sweden has created a multilevel learning system where local experimentation, citywide portfolios and national coordination inform one another through recurring cycles. The opportunity is to strengthen the links between learning and policy change, ensuring that implementation evidence systematically leads to regulatory and financial adjustments.
